idiom_name: duck-typed node objects with children arrays (Psych::Nodes as the stdlib instance)
implementation_notes: Ruby, like Python, needs no shared superclass: any object responding to the operation is a component, so a container is a duck-typed object holding an Array of children and a leaf is an object without children, with traversal written as each/block recursion. The standard library demonstrates the pattern directly - Psych::Nodes::Node is the base of a YAML node tree whose subclasses share a children array and an each that yields every node depth-first through Psych::Visitors - and REXML::Element does the same for XML. Introduce a base class or module when a shared initializer, hooks or an enforceable protocol are worth the coupling.
code_sketch:
class FileNode
  attr_reader :bytes
  def initialize(bytes) = @bytes = bytes
  def size = @bytes
end

class DirNode
  attr_reader :children
  def initialize(*children) = @children = children
  def size = children.sum(&:size)
  def each_node(&block)
    block.call(self)
    children.each { |child| child.each_node(&block) }
  end
end
pitfalls: A missing child method surfaces as NoMethodError at call time rather than at definition time; keep the protocol small and documented, or mix in a module that raises early.
Arrays are mutable and shared by reference, so two containers given the same array alias each other's subtrees.
Recursion is still recursion: a machine-generated chain thousands of nodes deep exhausts the stack, so large trees want an explicit stack.
